title: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Illinois | Basin Oil Owner Guide
metaDescription: Illinois Basin oil wells are old, shallow, and slow to decline. Learn how a stripper-well royalty check behaves and what it takes to sell your interest.
heroLead: Illinois Basin oil wells are mostly shallow, old, and slow-producing, which makes them some of the most predictable stripper wells in the country, and predictable is exactly what a buyer values.
intro: The Illinois Basin stretches across the southern third of the state, through counties like Marion, Clay, Wayne, Fayette, and Lawrence, and it has been producing oil since the early 1900s. Almost none of this is shale production; it is shallow conventional oil, often from sandstone reservoirs a few hundred to a couple thousand feet deep, produced through small pumping units known as stripper wells that each yield only a handful of barrels a day.

That shallow, low-volume, long-lived character shapes everything about an Illinois royalty check. This page walks through why these wells decline so slowly, what a typical Illinois division order looks like after a century of small transfers and inherited fractions, and what a fair offer on this kind of interest actually gets built from.

sections.heading: Shallow Wells, Slow Decline
paragraphs: Most Illinois Basin wells were drilled decades ago into shallow sandstone reservoirs, and many still on production today have been pumping for fifty years or more, often under waterflood to keep pressure up in the reservoir. Because these wells never had the high initial rates of a modern shale well, they also never had the steep early decline; the curve was gentle from the start and has stayed that way.

For an owner, this means a small but steady check that moves mostly with oil price rather than with a fast-changing production number. A stripper well producing three or four barrels a day today may have been producing four or five barrels a day a decade ago, which is a very different pattern than watching a shale well's output fall by half in its first year.

sections.heading: Small Interests, Many Owners
paragraphs: Illinois mineral tracts are often small to begin with, frequently tied to family farmland, and a century of inheritance has split many of them into fractional interests measured in the thousandths. It is common for an Illinois royalty check to represent a very small percentage of a well that itself only produces a few barrels a day, which means the checks themselves tend to be modest.

That does not mean the interest lacks value, particularly if the well has been producing reliably for decades, but it does mean the math is different than a headline-grabbing Permian well. We look at the whole picture, including how many other interests share the same tract, when we evaluate an Illinois offer.

sections.heading: Reading an Illinois Division Order
paragraphs: Illinois lease and division order records are typically held at the county recorder's office, and because so many of these leases date back generations, tracking the full ownership chain can take some digging, especially if the tract passed through probate without a clean deed. If your check comes through a small independent operator rather than a major company, it is also worth confirming the operator's own records match what you believe you own.
We regularly help Illinois owners pull and confirm this chain of title as part of putting together an offer, so you are not stuck trying to reconstruct a county's worth of old paperwork on your own.

sections.heading: What a Fair Offer on Illinois Stripper Production Looks Like
paragraphs: Because Illinois Basin wells have such long, well-documented production histories, they are often easier to price with confidence than a young well still working through its early volatile years. We build an offer from your actual royalty history, current oil pricing, and what similar Illinois stripper-well interests have recently traded for.
If your well has shown steady, unremarkable production for years, that consistency is a genuine asset for valuing your interest, not a downside.

faqs.question: Why does my Illinois oil check barely change from month to month?
faqs.answer: Illinois Basin wells are shallow, conventional, and were never high-rate to begin with, so they decline slowly and steadily rather than dropping sharply. Your check mostly tracks the price of oil rather than a fast-moving production number.

faqs.question: Is Illinois a shale oil state?
faqs.answer: No. Illinois Basin production is almost entirely shallow conventional oil from sandstone reservoirs, produced through small stripper wells, not horizontal shale wells.

faqs.question: Why is my Illinois royalty interest such a small fraction?
faqs.answer: Illinois mineral tracts tied to old family farmland have often split among many heirs over multiple generations, so an individual owner may hold a fractional interest measured in the thousandths of a small-producing well.

faqs.question: How do I confirm my Illinois ownership if the paperwork is old?
faqs.answer: Start with the deed and any division order on file with the county recorder and the operator. If the tract passed through probate without a clean deed, an attorney can help confirm the current chain of title.

faqs.question: What determines an offer on my Illinois interest?
faqs.answer: We look at your documented royalty history, current oil pricing, and recent comparable sales of Illinois Basin stripper-well interests. A long, steady production history is genuinely useful data, not a strike against the interest.
